text: Listen to an announcement from an economics professor.
script: W: Hello, everyone. This is Professor Alvarez with a quick update for Introduction to Economics.

W: Because the lecture hall will be used for a department event on Thursday, our midterm exam will not be held in class. Instead, I will post the exam online on Wednesday evening, and you will have forty-eight hours to submit your answers.
W: The exam is open book, but you must work alone. I will be checking answers for similarity, so please write everything in your own words.
W: If you have a disability accommodation or a problem with your internet connection, email me by Tuesday, and we will find another way for you to take it.
W: Thursday's class is cancelled, and we will meet again next Tuesday.

stem: Why will the midterm exam be handled differently this time?
options: The professor wants the exam to be shorter.
The department changed its rules about how exams are given.
Students asked for extra time to prepare.
The usual room will be needed for another event.
explanation: The speaker says the lecture hall 'will be used for a department event on Thursday', so the exam moves online. Nothing is said about its length, student requests or new department rules.

stem: What should a student with a connection problem do?
options: Come to the lecture hall on Thursday.
Write to the professor no later than Tuesday.
Wait until Wednesday evening to ask for help.
Hand the written answers to the department office.
explanation: The professor says to 'email me by Tuesday' if there is an internet problem. Thursday's class is cancelled, so there is no one in the hall, and Wednesday evening is when the exam is posted, which is too late to ask.

text: Listen to a phone message from a research assistant.
script: W: Hi, this is Mei Lin from the Sleep and Memory Lab, calling for people who signed up as volunteers last month.

W: We are starting a new study in two weeks, and we need adults between eighteen and thirty-five who normally sleep at least seven hours a night. The study has two visits. On the first visit, you will learn a list of word pairs. You will come back the next morning to be tested on them.
W: Each visit lasts about forty minutes, and participants receive twenty-five dollars in total.
W: Please call me back at extension four five one two, or reply to the email I sent today, to choose your time slots. Spaces are limited, so the sooner, the better.

stem: What is the main purpose of the message?
options: To invite earlier volunteers to join a new study.
To report the results of a recent memory experiment at the lab.
To change the time of a previous visit.
To ask volunteers to sleep longer each night.
explanation: The caller says she is calling people 'who signed up as volunteers last month' about 'a new study'. She does not give results or reschedule anything; seven hours of sleep is only a requirement for joining.

stem: What will participants do on the second visit?
options: Learn a new list of word pairs.
Fill in a form about how long they slept.
Take a test on what they learned before.
Collect the payment for the first visit.
explanation: On the first visit participants 'learn a list of word pairs', and they return 'the next morning to be tested on them'. Learning the list is the first visit, and payment is described as a single total of twenty-five dollars.

text: Listen to an announcement at a museum.
script: W: Welcome to the Harbor Maritime Museum. Before you begin your visit, we would like to share a few notes.

W: The main gallery, with the old sailing ships, is open all day. However, the lower level, which shows the tools of early navigators, is closed this week while we install new lighting. It will reopen on Monday.

W: Guided tours leave from the front desk at eleven and two. They last forty-five minutes and are included in your ticket. If you prefer to explore on your own, free audio guides are available in four languages.
W: Finally, please remember that flash photography is not allowed near the old maps, because bright light can damage them. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

stem: What does the speaker say about the lower level?
options: It has the largest collection of ships.
It cannot be visited until next week.
It requires a separate ticket for entry.
It is open only during guided tours.
explanation: The lower level 'is closed this week' for lighting work and 'will reopen on Monday'. The ships are in the main gallery, and the tours are included in the ticket, so the other options are not supported.

stem: Why are visitors asked not to use flash near the old maps?
options: It disturbs other visitors in the gallery.
The new lighting system could stop working.
Strong light could harm them.
Photographs of maps are not permitted at all.
explanation: The speaker says 'bright light can damage them'. The new lighting is mentioned only in connection with the lower level, and the rule is about flash, not about all photography.

text: Listen to a fire drill announcement in an office building.
script: W: Attention, everyone. This is a notice from the Building Safety Office about Wednesday's fire drill.

W: The alarm will sound at ten fifteen. When you hear it, stop what you are doing, leave your computer on, and walk to the nearest stairwell. Please do not use the elevators, even if you are on the top floor.
W: Once outside, gather in the parking area behind the building and wait for your floor warden to take attendance. Wardens will be wearing orange vests.

W: The drill will last about fifteen minutes. Staff who work from home on Wednesday do not need to take part, but they should read the safety checklist we emailed last week. Thank you for your cooperation.

stem: What should people do when the alarm sounds?
options: Look for a floor warden inside the building.
Turn off their computers and wait at their desks.
Take the elevator if they are on a high floor.
Go to a stairwell and leave on foot.
explanation: The speaker says to 'walk to the nearest stairwell' and not to use the elevators 'even if you are on the top floor'. Computers are to be left on, and wardens are met outside, not inside.

stem: What is true about employees who work from home on Wednesday?
options: They are asked to read a checklist.
They will receive an orange vest.
They must come to the parking area at ten fifteen.
They will do a separate drill online.
explanation: The announcement says they 'do not need to take part' but 'should read the safety checklist'. Orange vests belong to the wardens, and no online drill is mentioned.

text: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship.
script: W: Good afternoon. This is the Financial Aid Office with a reminder about the Global Citizens Scholarship.
W: The scholarship gives two thousand dollars to second-year students who have shown strong leadership in a community project. Applications are due by five p.m. on the fifteenth of March.
W: Your application must include a one-page essay and a letter from someone who has seen your project first-hand. Please note that a letter from a family member will not be accepted.

W: Last year, several students missed the deadline because they waited to ask for letters. We strongly suggest that you contact your references this week. Forms are available at the front counter and on our website.

stem: According to the announcement, what is required besides an essay?
options: Proof of a high grade point average.
A letter from someone who saw the project.
A report from the community organization you worked with.
A recommendation from a family friend.
explanation: The speaker says the application needs 'a letter from someone who has seen your project first-hand'. Grades are not mentioned, and only family members are specifically excluded; the organization does not write a report.

stem: Why does the speaker mention last year's students?
options: To encourage listeners to prepare early.
To show that the scholarship is easy to win.
To explain why the deadline was moved.
To praise students who finished early.
explanation: Several students 'missed the deadline because they waited to ask for letters', so the speaker advises contacting references this week. The deadline was not moved, and the point is a warning, not praise.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from a university housing office.
script: M: Hello, this is Daniel from the Student Housing Office, calling for Priya Nair.

M: I'm calling about your request to move to a quieter room. A single room has opened up in Birch Hall, on the second floor, and I wanted to offer it to you before I contact the next person on the list.
M: The room costs about eighty dollars more per month than your current one, but it has its own desk and a window facing the garden.

M: If you want it, please come to our office before noon on Friday and sign the new agreement. After that time, I will have to offer the room to someone else. You can also call me back at five five five, oh one four two. Thanks, and have a good day.

stem: Why is the man calling Priya?
options: To tell her that her room fee has gone up.
To ask her to leave Birch Hall early.
To check whether her desk is in good condition.
To offer her a room she had asked about.
explanation: He says he is calling 'about your request to move to a quieter room' and that a room 'has opened up'. The extra eighty dollars applies only to the new room, and nothing suggests she must leave.

stem: What will happen if Priya does nothing by Friday noon?
options: The housing office will call her again.
She will keep the room at a lower price.
The room may be given to another student.
Her request will be moved to the top of the list.
explanation: The man says 'after that time, I will have to offer the room to someone else'. He is already contacting the next person on the list, so there is no promise of another call or a better place in line.

text: Listen to an announcement at a conference.
script: W: Good morning, and welcome to the third day of the Regional Teaching Conference. I have a few updates about today's schedule.

W: The session on classroom technology has been moved from the Ballroom to Room C, because a larger group than expected has registered for the keynote speech in the Ballroom. The start time is the same, ten thirty.
W: Lunch will be served in the Garden Court from twelve until one thirty. Vegetarian meals are marked with a green card, so please look for them if you need one.
W: The shuttle to the hotels will leave from the main entrance at five, not five thirty as printed in your program. A later shuttle will leave at seven. Thank you, and enjoy your day.

stem: Why has the technology session been moved?
options: The speaker arrived at the conference late.
The ballroom is being cleaned in the morning.
Room C has better equipment for demonstrations.
A different event needs more space.
explanation: The room change is made because 'a larger group than expected has registered for the keynote speech in the Ballroom', so the keynote needs the space. The start time stays the same, and the speaker's arrival is never mentioned.

stem: What does the speaker say about the shuttle?
options: It now leaves from the Garden Court.
It will stop running after five o'clock.
A departure time was changed.
There is only one departure each evening.
explanation: The shuttle will leave 'at five, not five thirty as printed in your program', so the printed time is wrong. A later shuttle at seven also runs, which rules out the idea that service ends at five.

text: Listen to an announcement about campus construction.
script: M: Good afternoon. This is the Facilities Department with news about the work on the east side of campus.
M: Starting Monday, crews will begin replacing the pipes beneath Maple Walk, the path between the library and the Engineering Building. The walkway will be closed for about three weeks.

M: Students can still reach both buildings. Follow the yellow signs along Lake Road, which adds roughly five minutes to the walk. The library's main doors will stay open, but the side entrance facing Maple Walk will be locked.
M: We know that noise may be a problem for people studying nearby, so the loudest work will be done only between nine and eleven in the morning. We thank you for your patience.

stem: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To explain how repairs will affect students.
To ask students to avoid the library this month.
To invite students to a meeting about campus noise.
To announce that a new building will open soon.
explanation: The speaker describes the pipe replacement, the closed path and an alternative route, so the focus is how the work affects people. The library stays open, and no meeting or new building is mentioned.

stem: According to the speaker, how can students get to the Engineering Building during the work?
options: By crossing the library through its side entrance.
By following signs along a longer road.
By waiting until the loud work has finished.
By using Maple Walk before nine in the morning.
explanation: Students should 'follow the yellow signs along Lake Road', which 'adds roughly five minutes'. The side entrance will be locked, and the walkway is closed for three weeks, not just during noisy hours.

text: Listen to an announcement about a school sports event.
script: W: Hello, athletes and fans. This is Coach Rivera with news about Saturday's swimming meet.
W: Because of a problem with the heating system in our own pool, the meet will take place at Lakeside College instead. Warm-ups begin at eight thirty, and the first race is at nine thirty.
W: The college is about a thirty-minute drive away. A bus will leave from the gym parking lot at seven forty-five, and team members are expected to ride it, even if a parent is willing to drive them.
W: Spectators are welcome and tickets are free, but seating is limited, so please arrive early. Swimmers, remember to pack a towel, two swim caps, and your own water bottle. See you on Saturday.

stem: Why is the swimming meet being held at another location?
options: Too many spectators are expected at the school.
The visiting team requested a larger pool.
The home pool has an equipment problem.
The meet was scheduled for a different date.
explanation: Coach Rivera mentions 'a problem with the heating system in our own pool'. Spectators are welcome, but crowding is not the reason, and the date, Saturday, has not changed.

stem: What are team members expected to do?
options: Travel to the meet on the team bus.
Drive to Lakeside College with a parent.
Warm up at the gym before they leave.
Buy tickets for their family members.
explanation: The coach says team members 'are expected to ride it', meaning the bus, 'even if a parent is willing to drive them'. Warm-ups happen at the meet, and tickets are free.

text: Listen to an announcement from a history professor.
script: W: Before we finish for today, I'd like to say a few words about your research paper in this course.

W: Some of you have asked about choosing a topic outside the period we have studied. You can, but only if you first email me a short proposal, three or four sentences, explaining why the topic fits the themes of the course.
W: I should also mention that the library has reserved a shelf of books on trade routes. These are meant for everyone, so please do not take more than two at a time, and return them within a week.
W: The first draft is due in three weeks. A draft need not be perfect, but it should show a clear argument. I will return comments within seven days.

stem: What must a student do to choose a topic outside the period studied?
options: Ask the librarian for a special reading list.
Email the professor a short proposal.
Present the topic to the class for approval.
Submit the first draft three weeks early.
explanation: The professor says students can do this 'only if you first email me a short proposal' of a few sentences. The draft deadline and the library shelf are separate matters, and there is no class vote.

stem: Why does the professor mention the shelf of books on trade routes?
options: To warn that the library is short of space.
To say that the topic is required for all papers.
To recommend books for the final exam.
To remind students to share the books fairly.
explanation: She says the books are 'meant for everyone', so students should take no more than two at a time. Trade routes are only one possible topic, and the books are not linked to an exam.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from a professor to a student.
script: M: Hi Kwame, this is Professor Lindqvist returning your call about the geology field report.

M: I looked at the outline you sent, and the structure is good. My only concern is the section on rock samples. You describe where you found each sample, but you don't yet explain what the samples tell us about the history of the valley, and that is the main goal of the assignment.
M: I'd suggest you spend some time in my office hours this week. Bring your notes and the photographs from the trip, and we can go through them together.
M: I'm in my office on Wednesday from two to four, or Thursday morning by appointment. Let me know which works for you. Talk soon.

stem: What does the professor think of Kwame's outline?
options: It is too short to meet the requirements.
It does not include enough photographs.
Well organized, but one part is weak.
It has too many details about the valley.
explanation: He says 'the structure is good' but is worried about the rock sample section, which describes places and does not yet explain what the samples show. Photographs are things to bring to the meeting, not a fault in the outline.

stem: What does the professor suggest Kwame do?
options: Collect more rock samples from the valley.
Write the report during office hours.
Send his notes by email before Wednesday.
Meet him to go over the materials.
explanation: The professor says to 'spend some time in my office hours' with notes and photographs so 'we can go through them together'. He does not ask for new samples or for the report to be written in his office.

text: Listen to an announcement about a research study.
script: W: Hello, everyone. I'm Dr. Hassan, and I'm looking for volunteers for a study on how people choose what to eat in a cafeteria.

W: The study takes place in the Student Center, and you need no preparation. You will simply have lunch as you normally would, while a small camera above the food stations records which foods you look at and select.
W: No one will see the recordings except the research team, and your name will not be attached to them. After lunch, you will answer five short questions about your choices.
W: Volunteers receive a free meal and a coupon for a coffee. If you can join us on Tuesday or Thursday between noon and one, please speak to the assistant at the table outside this room.

stem: What is the study mainly about?
options: How people make food choices.
Whether cafeterias serve healthy meals.
How cameras change people's habits.
Which foods students enjoy the most.
explanation: Dr. Hassan says it is about 'how people choose what to eat in a cafeteria'. The camera is only a tool for recording, and the speaker never says that the foods will be rated for health or taste.

stem: What will volunteers receive for taking part?
options: Money for each question answered.
A meal and a coupon.
A copy of their own recordings.
Credit toward a psychology course.
explanation: The speaker says 'volunteers receive a free meal and a coupon for a coffee'. Recordings stay with the research team, and no money or course credit is mentioned.

text: Listen to a notice from a guided tour company.
script: W: Thank you for choosing Old Town Walking Tours. Before we begin, here are a few details about this morning's tour.

W: We will walk about three kilometers over two hours, mostly on flat streets, with a short stop at the market square. If anyone prefers a slower pace, please tell me now, and I will arrange for a second guide to walk with you at the back.
W: Our route passes the old clock tower, which was built in the fifteenth century. Normally we climb to the top, but the stairs are being repaired, so we will view it from the square instead.
W: Please keep your belongings close in crowded areas. Restrooms are available at the market, and we will meet here again at noon.

stem: What can people who want to walk slowly do?
options: Skip the market square stop.
Ask for another guide to join them.
Take a shorter tour in the afternoon.
Wait for the group at the clock tower.
explanation: The guide says she will 'arrange for a second guide to walk with you at the back'. The stop at the market is for everyone, and the clock tower is seen from the square, not used as a waiting place.

stem: What is different about today's visit to the clock tower?
options: A new guide will explain its history.
The tower will be closed to all visitors.
The group will see it later at noon.
The group will not go up inside it.
explanation: Usually 'we climb to the top, but the stairs are being repaired, so we will view it from the square instead'. The tower is not closed to viewing, and the noon meeting is the end of the tour.

text: Listen to a safety announcement in a chemistry laboratory.
script: M: Before you start your experiments today, I need your attention for a short safety reminder.

M: Last week, someone left a bottle of solvent open on the shared bench. Nobody was hurt, but the smell filled the room, and we had to open all the windows. From now on, every bottle must be closed and returned to the cabinet as soon as you finish with it.
M: Also, goggles must be worn at all times, even if you are only writing notes at your bench. Regular glasses are not a substitute.
M: If you spill anything, don't try to wipe it up with paper towels. Raise your hand, and one of the assistants will bring the right equipment. Thank you, and good luck with today's work.

stem: Why does the speaker mention the open bottle?
options: To report an injury that happened last week.
To ask who left the windows closed.
To explain why a rule is being stressed.
To praise students for acting quickly.
explanation: The incident is the reason for the new instruction that 'every bottle must be closed and returned to the cabinet'. The speaker says nobody was hurt, and the windows were opened, not left closed.

stem: What should a student do after spilling a chemical?
options: Ask an assistant to deal with it.
Clean it with a few paper towels.
Open the windows and leave the room.
Put the bottle back in the cabinet.
explanation: The speaker says not to use paper towels but to 'raise your hand' so an assistant brings the right equipment. Returning bottles to the cabinet is the rule for finishing work, not for spills.

text: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship program.
script: W: Hello, students. This message is from the Office of International Programs.

W: Applications are now open for the Horizon Exchange Scholarship, which pays for one semester of study abroad. To apply, you need a grade point average of three point two or higher and at least two semesters left at this university.
W: The application has two parts. The online form is due on the first of April. Finalists will then be interviewed in the second week of April, and decisions will be sent by email on the thirtieth.

W: An information session will be held next Wednesday at four in the Global Lounge. You do not need to register for it, but we would encourage you to bring your questions. Past winners will be there to share their experiences.

stem: What happens after the online form is submitted?
options: Every applicant receives a decision by email.
Applicants send a second form in April.
Winners attend an information session.
Some applicants are invited to an interview.
explanation: The speaker says 'finalists will then be interviewed' in the second week of April; only after that are decisions sent. The information session comes before the deadline, and there is no second form.

stem: What is the purpose of the information session?
options: To answer questions and share experiences.
To interview students who have applied.
To explain the rules of the study-abroad courses.
To register for the scholarship competition.
explanation: She says to 'bring your questions' and that 'past winners will be there to share their experiences'. Registration is not needed, and interviews are held later, in April.

text: Listen to an announcement from an art history professor.
script: W: Good morning, everyone. Before we look at today's slides, I have news about our class trip to the City Gallery.

W: The visit is next Friday, and we will meet at the gallery entrance at ten, not in our classroom. The gallery is offering us a private talk with one of its curators about the paintings from the nineteenth century, which we have been studying.

W: Admission is free for our group, but you must show your student card at the door. If you cannot attend because of another class, send me an email, and I will give you a short written assignment on the same paintings instead.
W: Please wear comfortable shoes, since we will be standing for most of the hour.

stem: What will students do on the trip?
options: Paint copies of famous works in the gallery.
Attend a class in a classroom at ten.
Hear a gallery expert talk about paintings.
Interview artists about modern techniques.
explanation: The professor says the gallery offers 'a private talk with one of its curators' about nineteenth-century paintings. The class meets at the gallery, not in the classroom, and no painting or interviews are mentioned.

stem: What can a student who has another class do?
options: Visit the gallery on a different day.
Write about the same works.
Join the trip after the curator's talk.
Ask the curator to repeat the talk.
explanation: She says she will 'give you a short written assignment on the same paintings instead'. Nothing is said about a later visit or a second talk.

text: Listen to an announcement at a research conference.
script: M: Good evening, delegates. Here is some information about tomorrow's poster session.

M: The session takes place in the Exhibition Hall from four to six. If you are presenting, you may begin setting up your poster at three. Pins will be provided at each board, so you don't need to bring your own.
M: Please look at the number on your name badge. That number is the board you have been given. Please don't move to a different board, even if it seems to have more space.

M: Judges will walk through the hall at about four thirty, so stay near your poster during that time. Light refreshments will be served at the back of the hall, and we ask that no food or drink be carried near the posters.

stem: What should presenters use to find their poster board?
options: The title of their research paper.
The number on their badge.
A map posted outside the hall.
A list provided by the judges.
explanation: The speaker says 'the number on your name badge' is 'the board you have been given'. Titles, maps and the judges' list are not mentioned.

stem: What is implied about the judges' walk through the hall?
options: They will begin before setup is finished.
They will give prizes for the best refreshments.
Presenters need to be at their boards then.
They will stay in the hall until six.
explanation: Judges 'will walk through the hall at about four thirty, so stay near your poster during that time'. Setup is allowed from three, so it is done earlier, and nothing is said about how long judges stay.

text: Listen to an announcement about parking on campus.
script: W: Attention, students and staff who drive to campus. This is an update from the Parking Office.

W: Starting next Monday, Lot B, the large lot next to the gym, will be closed for resurfacing. The work should take two weeks. During this time, drivers with a Lot B permit may park in Lot D without paying any extra fee.
W: Lot D is a ten-minute walk from the main buildings, so a free shuttle will run every fifteen minutes from seven in the morning until six at night. The shuttle stop is at the corner of Pine Street.
W: Please note that cars left in Lot B after Sunday night will be moved at the owner's expense. Thank you.

stem: Who is the announcement mainly intended for?
options: Drivers with Lot B permits.
Drivers who park on Pine Street.
Staff who have never bought a permit.
Visitors who use the gym on weekends.
explanation: The speaker says 'drivers with a Lot B permit may park in Lot D', and the whole message is about the Lot B closing. Gym visitors and Pine Street are only mentioned in passing, and permit-less drivers are not addressed.

stem: What will happen to a car left in Lot B after Sunday night?
options: It will be taken to the shuttle stop.
It will be parked in Lot D at no cost.
It will remain there during the work.
It will be moved at its owner's cost.
explanation: The final warning is that such cars 'will be moved at the owner's expense'. The free parking is for those who move their cars themselves, and the work needs the lot to be empty.

text: Listen to an announcement about an intramural sports event.
script: W: Hello, everyone. This is the Recreation Center with details about the intramural soccer tournament.
W: Registration closes this Friday at five. Each team needs between eight and twelve players, and at least three players on every team must be first-year students. That rule is new this year.
W: Games will be played on Saturdays in October, and the schedule will be posted on our website next week. The team with the most points at the end of the month will win a trophy and a pizza party.
W: If you want to play but don't have a team, come to the front desk, and we will help match you with other players. Teams without enough players by Friday will be dropped from the tournament.

stem: What is new about the tournament this year?
options: A lower number of teams in total.
A first-year player minimum.
A pizza party for all players.
Games on weekdays instead of weekends.
explanation: The speaker says 'at least three players on every team must be first-year students' and adds 'That rule is new this year'. The pizza party is for the winners only, and the games remain on Saturdays.

stem: What should a student without a team do?
options: Come to the games and join any team.
Wait for the schedule to be posted online.
Register as a team of eight players.
Ask the staff at the front desk for help.
explanation: The staff 'will help match you with other players' at the front desk. The schedule is for registered teams, and registering as a team requires finding the players first.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from a library.
script: M: Hello, this is Marcus from the Lakeside College Library, calling for Yuki Tanaka.
M: On Tuesday, you reserved a study room for Thursday afternoon, but unfortunately, there is a problem. The air conditioning in that room has stopped working, and the repair will not be done by then.

M: We have two choices for you. You could take our larger room on the third floor at the same time, though it has no screen for presentations. Or you could keep the original room if you don't mind the heat, and we would provide a fan.
M: Please call us back at extension two two one eight, or stop by the front desk before Wednesday evening, and tell us which you prefer. Thanks for your understanding.

stem: What is the main reason for the call?
options: To remind Yuki to return a late book.
To invite Yuki to a presentation on Thursday.
To report a problem with her booking.
To ask Yuki to pay a fee for a room.
explanation: Marcus says a reserved room has 'a problem' because the air conditioning is broken. Nothing is said about overdue books, invitations, or payments.

stem: What is a disadvantage of the larger room?
options: It has no screen.
It is farther from the front desk.
It is warmer than the original room.
It is available only in the morning.
explanation: The man says the larger room 'has no screen for presentations'. The time is the same, and the heat belongs to the original room.

text: Listen to an announcement from a linguistics professor.
script: M: Hi, everyone. Two quick things before you leave today.

M: First, the recording project. Each pair needs to record a ten-minute conversation in natural speech. I know some of you have worried that your recording will sound too formal. Please try to forget the microphone, talk about something you care about, and don't prepare a script.

M: Second, our guest. Next week, instead of my usual lecture, Dr. Ivanova from the Language Technology Institute will talk about how computers learn to recognize accents. Her visit was arranged only yesterday, so it isn't on the syllabus.
M: There will be a short quiz on her talk the following Monday, so take careful notes. I'll post the recording project instructions online tonight.

stem: What does the professor advise students to do for the recording?
options: Practice a ten-minute dialogue in advance.
Use a formal style to sound professional.
Record in a place without any other voices.
Speak naturally, with no script.
explanation: He says to 'forget the microphone, talk about something you care about, and don't prepare a script'. A formal style is the thing students worry about, not the goal.

stem: What can be inferred about the guest talk?
options: It was arranged at short notice.
It will replace the recording project.
It is part of the regular syllabus.
It will be recorded for the quiz.
explanation: The professor says her visit 'was arranged only yesterday, so it isn't on the syllabus'. The talk takes the place of one lecture, not the project, and the quiz is about the talk, not a recording of it.

text: Listen to a phone message asking for volunteers for a survey.
script: W: Hello, this is Amara from the Parks and Recreation Department. I'm calling members of our neighborhood group about a survey this weekend.

W: We are counting how many people use Riverside Park, and at what times of day. We need volunteers to stand at the four park entrances for two hours each and mark a tally sheet every time someone walks or cycles in.
W: No special skills are needed, but because it may be cool by the water, we recommend a warm jacket. We will provide clipboards, pens, and snacks.

W: The shifts are Saturday and Sunday mornings and afternoons. If you can help, please text your name and your preferred shift to five five five, oh one nine nine. Thank you so much for supporting your park.

stem: What will the volunteers do?
options: Ask visitors about their opinions of the park.
Count visitors as they enter the park.
Clean the areas around the entrances.
Hand out information about local clubs.
explanation: Volunteers will 'mark a tally sheet every time someone walks or cycles in' at the entrances. A tally records numbers only; they do not interview visitors or clean.

stem: How should interested people respond?
options: By calling the department on Monday.
By visiting the park office on Saturday.
By texting their name and shift.
By emailing the neighborhood group.
explanation: The caller says to 'text your name and your preferred shift' to the given number. Saturday is when the survey takes place, not a time for signing up.

text: Listen to an announcement at a planetarium.
script: W: Welcome to the Starfield Planetarium. We are pleased to have you with us this afternoon.

W: In a few minutes, our program, Journey Through the Solar System, will begin in the main dome. The show lasts thirty-five minutes. Latecomers cannot be admitted after the lights go down, because sudden light from the doorway affects everyone's view of the stars.
W: If you have a child under five, you may prefer our short show, Little Stars, which is shown in the smaller theater at one thirty and three. It has softer music and shorter scenes.
W: Please turn your phones off or set them to silent. And remember that our gift shop closes thirty minutes before the last show.

stem: Why can't latecomers enter after the show begins?
options: The seats are given to people on a waiting list.
Younger children might be frightened in the dark.
The program is too short to repeat a scene.
Light from the door would spoil the experience.
explanation: The speaker says 'sudden light from the doorway affects everyone's view of the stars'. Children are mentioned only in connection with the other show, and nothing is said about a waiting list.

stem: Who is the Little Stars show designed for?
options: Visitors who arrive after the lights go down.
Families with very young children.
Adults who want a longer program.
Students who study astronomy.
explanation: She suggests it for 'a child under five' and says it has softer music and shorter scenes. Late arrivals are not admitted to the main show, and the little show is the shorter one.

text: Listen to an announcement about a campus safety service.
script: M: Good evening, this is Campus Security with a reminder about the night walking escort service.

M: If you are on campus after nine p.m. and feel uncomfortable walking alone, you can request an escort. Just call the number on the back of your student card, or press the blue button on any of the emergency phones near the paths.

M: A trained student officer will meet you where you are, usually within ten minutes, and walk with you to your residence hall or to the parking lot. The service is free and is available every night until two in the morning.
M: Last term, officers accompanied more than five hundred students. You do not need a special reason to use it. We would rather you call than walk alone.

stem: How can students ask for an escort?
options: By sending a message from their residence hall.
By going to the security office in person.
By calling or pressing a button.
By signing up a day in advance online.
explanation: The speaker says to 'call the number on the back of your student card, or press the blue button' on the emergency phones. Nothing is mentioned about visiting the office or booking ahead.

stem: What does the speaker imply about using the service?
options: No serious reason is required.
It is mostly used by new students each term.
It may be unavailable when the officers are busy.
It is meant only for emergencies after midnight.
explanation: He says 'You do not need a special reason' and 'We would rather you call than walk alone', which suggests that students should not hesitate. The service runs until two, not just after midnight, and there is no mention of unavailability.

text: Listen to an announcement about a research grant for undergraduates.
script: W: Hello, everyone. This is Dr. Osei from the Undergraduate Research Office.

W: We are now accepting proposals for the Summer Research Grant. This grant gives up to three thousand dollars to students who want to carry out a research project of their own with a faculty mentor, between June and August.
W: Before you apply, you must find a professor willing to be your mentor. Without a signed mentor form, your application will not be considered, so start that conversation soon.

W: Proposals should be two pages long and explain not only what you plan to study but also why it matters. The deadline is the twentieth of February. We will hold a workshop on proposal writing on the sixth, in Room one fourteen of the library.

stem: What must students have before applying?
options: A completed project from last summer.
A two-page report on their grades.
A letter from the research office.
A willing faculty mentor.
explanation: She says students 'must find a professor willing to be your mentor' and that a signed form is needed. The two pages are the proposal, not a report on grades.

stem: What is the purpose of the workshop on the sixth?
options: To match students with professors.
To announce which students were chosen.
To help students write proposals.
To review work done during the summer.
explanation: The workshop is described as 'a workshop on proposal writing'. The matching is something students do themselves, and the deadline in February comes before any summer work.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from a computer science teaching assistant.
script: W: Hi everyone, this is Sofia, the teaching assistant for Computer Science one fifty. I'm leaving this message for all students in Thursday's lab section.

W: Our lab this week has a different format. Instead of working on the programming exercise in the computer room, we will meet in Room two eleven for a code review. Each of you should bring a printed copy of your last assignment, and you will explain your solution to a classmate.
W: The point is not to find mistakes but to practice describing your thinking clearly. It will not be graded, but attendance will be recorded.
W: If you have not submitted your last assignment yet, please do it today, so that you have something to discuss. Thanks, and see you Thursday.

stem: What will students do in this week's lab?
options: Explain their solutions to each other.
Write a new program at a computer.
Correct errors in their classmates' work.
Take a graded test on programming.
explanation: Students will 'explain your solution to a classmate' in a code review. The speaker says the purpose is 'not to find mistakes' and the session 'will not be graded'.

stem: Why does the teaching assistant ask students to submit their assignment today?
options: Because the lab room is being changed.
So they will have work to talk about.
Because attendance depends on it.
So she can grade it before Thursday.
explanation: She says to submit it 'so that you have something to discuss'. Attendance is recorded separately, and the review is not graded.

text: Listen to an announcement at a conference registration desk.
script: M: Welcome to the International Business Forum. If you are listening to this message, you are probably in line for registration, so let me explain how it works.

M: There are two lines. People whose last names begin with A through L should use the left desk, and everyone else should use the right desk. Please have your confirmation email ready, either on your phone or printed.
M: After you register, you will receive a badge, a program, and a meal ticket. Your badge is required to enter all sessions, so please wear it at all times.
M: If you ordered a conference T-shirt, you can collect it from the table by the stairs, not at the registration desk. Thank you for your patience.

stem: What do people need to do while waiting?
options: Choose a shirt size at the stairs.
Prepare their confirmation email.
Write their name on a meal ticket.
Learn which sessions they can enter.
explanation: The speaker asks people to 'have your confirmation email ready, either on your phone or printed'. The shirts are collected later at a different table, and the badge, not the ticket, gives access to sessions.

stem: Where can attendees pick up a conference T-shirt?
options: At the meal ticket counter.
At the left registration desk.
At the right registration desk.
At a table near the stairs.
explanation: The speaker says to collect it 'from the table by the stairs, not at the registration desk'. Both registration desks are therefore wrong, and no meal ticket counter is mentioned.

text: Listen to an announcement about renovations in a residence hall.
script: W: Hello, residents of Cedar Hall. This message comes from the Residence Life Office.

W: Beginning next week, the north elevator will be out of service for about a month while it is being modernized. The south elevator will remain open, but we expect longer waiting times in the morning and evening.

W: If you live on the first or second floor, please use the stairs, so people living on higher floors or with mobility needs can use the elevator more easily. Residents who cannot use stairs can contact the front desk to arrange a room on the ground floor temporarily.
W: We also ask you not to move large furniture during the work. The elevator will return before the end of the month.

stem: Why are first and second floor residents asked to take the stairs?
options: To leave room in the elevator for others.
Because their floors have no elevator access.
To help workers finish earlier.
Because the stairs have just been repaired.
explanation: She says to use the stairs 'so people living on higher floors or with mobility needs can use the elevator more easily'. Nothing is said about repairs to the stairs or the work schedule.

stem: What can residents who cannot use the stairs do?
options: Move to a different residence hall.
Wait for the north elevator to open.
Ask for a ground-floor room.
Use the elevator only in the morning.
explanation: The announcement says they can 'contact the front desk to arrange a room on the ground floor temporarily'. The north elevator is closed for a month, and the south elevator is open at all times.

text: Listen to an announcement about a community fun run.
script: W: Hello, runners and walkers. This is Hye-jin from the City Fitness Club, with the final details for Sunday's charity fun run.

W: The five-kilometer course starts at the clock tower and finishes at Memorial Field. Roads along the route will be closed from seven thirty, so please do not try to drive near the course. The run begins at eight.

W: You can collect your race number at the club until Saturday at six. If you are late, you can still pick it up on Sunday, but only from half past six until seven fifteen, and queues are likely to be long.
W: Every runner will receive a medal, and all the money raised goes to the children's hospital. We hope the weather stays dry.

stem: Why does the speaker tell people not to drive near the course?
options: Because parking is free at the club.
Because the roads will be shut.
Because the run starts earlier than planned.
Because the finish line has moved.
explanation: She says roads 'will be closed from seven thirty'. The run starts at eight as planned, and the club is where numbers are collected, not a free parking lot.

stem: What is implied about collecting a race number on Sunday morning?
options: It is forbidden for all runners.
It is faster than collecting it on Saturday.
It is only for children and walkers.
It is possible but may be inconvenient.
explanation: Late runners 'can still pick it up on Sunday' in a narrow window, and 'queues are likely to be long'. This suggests it works but is not ideal; it is neither forbidden nor quicker.

text: Listen to a tour announcement at a botanical garden.
script: M: Good morning, and welcome to the Greenfield Botanical Garden. I'll be your guide on today's walk.

M: We will start in the tropical greenhouse, where the air is warm and humid, so you might want to take off your jackets. After about twenty minutes, we'll move outside to the herb garden, where you are welcome to touch and smell the plants.
M: Please remember that some plants in the garden are rare, and a few can irritate the skin, so only touch those that have a green tag. The ones with a red tag are for looking only.
M: The walk ends at the garden cafe, around eleven fifteen. Anyone who has to leave early may do so, but let me know first.

stem: What does the guide suggest people do in the greenhouse?
options: Stay for the entire morning.
Touch the plants with green tags.
Remove their jackets.
Carry their bags in front of them.
explanation: He says the air is 'warm and humid, so you might want to take off your jackets'. Touching is welcomed in the herb garden, which comes after the greenhouse.

stem: What does a red tag on a plant mean?
options: Visitors should not touch it.
It is a plant from a tropical country.
It can be picked and taken away.
It will be sold at the cafe.
explanation: The guide says 'the ones with a red tag are for looking only', since some plants are rare or can irritate the skin. Green tags are the plants that visitors may touch.

text: Listen to an announcement from a sociology professor.
script: W: Before I let you go, a note about the survey assignment. most groups have chosen to ask classmates about their social media habits. That's convenient, but it's also why I'm going to be strict about one thing.

W: A sample drawn only from this course won't tell you anything about students at the university as a whole. We'll discuss that on Monday, and I'll expect your reports to address it directly, whether or not you fix it.

W: Anyone willing to go beyond the classroom is welcome to use the lounge in the student union on Wednesday afternoon. The union lets us approach people there, provided we ask permission first and stay under an hour.
W: Of course, this is optional. But I would think carefully before dismissing it.

stem: Why does the professor mention the limitation of the sample?
options: To signal something she will grade.
To explain why the survey was cancelled.
To discourage them from studying social media.
To suggest that classmates dislike surveys.
explanation: She says she will 'expect your reports to address it directly', which signals it will count in the evaluation. She never discourages the topic, and the survey continues.

stem: What does the professor imply when she says she would 'think carefully before dismissing' the optional activity?
options: The union may soon withdraw permission.
Those who do it will gain an edge.
The optional activity is actually required.
Using the lounge is dangerous for students.
explanation: The activity lets students collect a wider sample, which addresses the flaw she has just described, so those who do it will have a stronger report. It is explicitly 'optional', so it is not required, and the permission is described without any warning of withdrawal.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from a volunteer coordinator.
script: M: Hello, this is Tomas from the Riverside Language Exchange, returning your message about volunteering as a conversation partner.

M: I appreciate your offer, and your experience teaching would certainly be an asset. However, I should be upfront about one thing. Our sessions are usually held in the evening, and most volunteers commit to a whole semester, because the learners build trust with one particular partner over time.

M: If your schedule makes that difficult, I could add you to our short-notice list instead. Those volunteers cover for absent partners, so there are fewer hours, but it can lead to a regular placement in the next term.
M: Give me a call back at your convenience, and we can talk through which arrangement suits you best.

stem: What is the purpose of the message?
options: To reject the caller's application politely.
To arrange a meeting with a language learner.
To explain options after an offer to help.
To ask for teaching experience references.
explanation: Tomas responds to an offer and then explains a regular commitment and a short-notice option. He welcomes the experience, so he is not rejecting anything, and no meeting or references are requested.

stem: Why does the coordinator mention that learners build trust?
options: To say that new volunteers work with several partners.
To show that the short-notice list is full.
To suggest that the caller should give lessons.
To explain why a long commitment is preferred.
explanation: Volunteers are asked to commit for a whole semester 'because the learners build trust with one particular partner over time'. The same sentence rules out several partners, and the short-notice list is described as an available option.

text: Listen to a talk by a museum guide at the start of a tour.
script: W: Thank you for joining me. Since several of you asked about the glass cases, let me explain why this wing looks the way it does.

W: These manuscripts are over six hundred years old, and light is their greatest enemy. That is why the room is so dim, and why we rotate the displays every three months. A page that you see today may not be available when you return in the spring.
W: You'll notice that a few pages are shown only as high-quality copies. The originals are in storage, and come out only for researchers.
W: Many visitors say the copies let them look more closely, since they can be enlarged on the screens at the end of the hall.

stem: What can be inferred about the displays in the room?
options: They rotate to protect fragile items.
They are unchanged since the museum opened.
They are always shown in bright light.
They are copies of lost manuscripts.
explanation: The speaker says light is the manuscripts' 'greatest enemy' and displays are rotated 'every three months', so they are protected by regular change. The statement about copies refers to only a few pages.

stem: Why does the guide mention the screens at the end of the hall?
options: To explain how researchers apply for access.
To warn visitors that the tour will run late.
To promote a collection of film recordings.
To suggest a benefit of seeing the copies.
explanation: Right after admitting that some pages are copies, she says visitors 'can look more closely' because copies can be enlarged on the screens. This answers possible disappointment, and has nothing to do with the researchers' application.

text: Listen to a safety announcement before an evacuation drill.
script: M: Good morning, everyone. As you know, we will be practicing our evacuation procedure at half past ten. I would like to address a few common mistakes we noticed in the previous drill.

M: First, many people stopped to collect their coats and bags. In a real situation, those seconds matter, and it is better to leave everything behind. Second, a number of staff held the doors open for others after the alarm, which blocks the safe closing of fire doors. Close every door behind you.
M: Finally, please resist the temptation to gather at the building entrance. Those who stand there prevent others from leaving, and make it harder for firefighters to arrive.
M: Move to the field, past the white line, and wait for instructions. Thank you.

stem: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To announce a change in the time of the drill.
To correct mistakes seen in the last drill.
To explain how fire doors are manufactured.
To thank staff for their quick action.
explanation: The speaker says he wants to 'address a few common mistakes we noticed in the previous drill'. The time is only mentioned as background, and the staff behavior is criticized, not praised.

stem: What does the speaker want people to do after the alarm?
options: Wait by the entrance for the firefighters.
Hold the doors open until others pass.
Shut doors and go to the field.
Go back for personal items if it is safe.
explanation: He asks them to 'close every door behind you' and to 'move to the field, past the white line'. Holding doors, gathering at the entrance, and collecting belongings are the mistakes he lists.

text: Listen to an announcement about scholarship requirements.
script: W: Good afternoon. This message is for students who currently hold the Merit Scholarship.

W: Renewal for next year is not automatic. To keep your award, you must complete at least thirty credits and maintain a grade point average of three point oh. Students who fall short by even a small margin will receive a letter, and the committee will review their situation individually.

W: I want to be clear that this is not a formality. In the past two years, a fifth of recipients lost their funding, and most of them could have appealed. The deadline for appeals is the first Friday of the next semester, and late appeals are not considered.
W: If you are uncertain about where you stand, the advising office can calculate your figures with you.

stem: What is the speaker's main concern?
options: That the grading system has changed.
That fewer students are applying for scholarships.
That the committee has become too strict.
That recipients misunderstand renewal rules.
explanation: She stresses that renewal 'is not a formality' and that many recipients lost funding although they 'could have appealed', so the worry is a lack of awareness. Application numbers and grading changes are never discussed.

stem: What should a student with a lower grade point average do?
options: Make an appeal before the stated deadline.
Wait for the committee to contact them.
Complete additional credits in the summer.
Ask the advising office to submit a new application.
explanation: A letter will be sent and the committee reviews cases, but the speaker says the recipients 'could have appealed' and that the appeal deadline is strict. The advising office only helps calculate figures.

text: Listen to an announcement from a biology professor.
script: M: A reminder about next week's field trip to the wetlands. The bus leaves at seven, and I know that's early, but the tide determines our schedule, not me.
M: The best time to observe the birds is when the water is low, and that happens before nine. If we arrive later, the mud flats will be covered, and there will be little to see except water.
M: Bring boots, because the ground will be wet, and bring your field guides. The binoculars belong to the department, so I'll hand them out on arrival and expect them back.
M: Anyone who cannot make the early departure should speak to me today. Please don't simply arrive at eight, expecting to join us.

stem: Why does the professor say the tide determines the schedule?
options: The bus drivers must follow the tide tables.
Birds show up at low water.
The wetlands close to visitors at nine.
The binoculars have to be returned by nine.
explanation: The best time for observing is 'when the water is low', before nine, and later 'the mud flats will be covered'. The bus and binoculars are unrelated to tides.

stem: What does the professor imply about students arriving at eight?
options: They will receive a different assignment.
They can join if they bring their own boots.
They will have missed the group.
They must request special permission in writing.
explanation: He asks them not to 'simply arrive at eight, expecting to join us', as the group has left at seven and the water will be rising. Speaking to him today is what he asks for, not a written form.

text: Listen to a phone message about a psychology experiment.
script: W: Hello, this is Dr. Ng's lab calling for Lucas Moreau. Thank you for completing our online screening questionnaire.

W: Based on your answers, you qualify for the next stage of our study on attention. I should mention that the study involves wearing a small headband that measures brain activity. It is painless and harmless, but some people find it uncomfortable around the forehead, so we like to mention it beforehand.
W: The session lasts an hour and pays thirty dollars. If you are still interested, please do not drink coffee or energy drinks for four hours before you arrive. Caffeine can change the readings.
W: To book a time, reply to this number by text, and we'll send you directions.

stem: Why does the caller mention the headband?
options: Because it causes pain in some people.
To explain how the questionnaire was scored.
Because it must be returned after use.
So Lucas can decide if he minds.
explanation: The headband is 'painless and harmless', but 'some people find it uncomfortable', which is why the lab 'like[s] to mention it beforehand' so he can decide. The scoring of the questionnaire is a separate subject.

stem: Why are participants told to avoid caffeine?
options: It could affect the measurements.
It would make the session too long.
It is not allowed in the lab building.
It reduces the payment they receive.
explanation: She says 'Caffeine can change the readings'. The session length and payment are given separately, and no building rule is mentioned.

text: Listen to a notice about changes at a science museum.
script: W: Visitors, please note that the Hall of Origins will be closed for the next two weeks. We know many of you came to see it.

W: While the hall is closed, we have opened a temporary display in the lobby, which includes a few of the smaller fossils, though not the large skeleton at the entrance. Tickets for this week and next are half price, and your ticket will also be valid for a return visit within six months.
W: If you have purchased a ticket for a guided tour of the Hall of Origins, you will receive a refund at the front desk, or you may exchange it for a tour of the Planet Gallery.
W: Thank you for your understanding.

stem: What can be inferred about the large skeleton?
options: It has been moved to the lobby.
It is damaged and needs repair.
It is unavailable for now.
It is too large for the Planet Gallery.
explanation: The lobby display has smaller fossils 'though not the large skeleton at the entrance', and the hall is closed, so it is unavailable. The announcement gives no reason like damage.

stem: What can someone with a tour ticket for the closed hall do?
options: Use the ticket in six months only.
Get a refund or switch tours.
Visit the lobby display for free.
Take a self-guided walk through the hall.
explanation: The announcement offers 'a refund at the front desk' or an exchange 'for a tour of the Planet Gallery'. The six-month validity applies to regular tickets bought at half price.

text: Listen to an announcement about a graduate scholarship.
script: M: This is a message for those considering the Hartwell Fellowship. The committee has asked me to clarify a few points that cause confusion.

M: The fellowship supports one year of study, but it is not a general scholarship. Applicants must propose a project that connects two academic fields, such as economics and public health. A strong grade record alone will not be enough.

M: Letters of recommendation must come from professors who know your work, not from friends or employers, however impressive their titles. The application closes on the first of November, and no extension is possible, since the committee meets the following week.
M: We recommend that you begin the proposal now, even if the plan is not final.

stem: What kind of applicant is the fellowship intended for?
options: Someone with the highest grades in a field.
Someone seeking money for several years.
Someone who already works in public health.
Someone planning a two-field project.
explanation: Applicants 'must propose a project that connects two academic fields', and grades alone 'will not be enough'. The fellowship supports 'one year of study', not several.

stem: Why does the speaker say no extension is possible?
options: Late applications were abused in the past.
The committee meets right afterward.
The recommenders need time to write letters.
The proposal must be finished by the committee.
explanation: The speaker links the deadline to the committee meeting 'the following week'. Nothing is said about past misuse, and the letters come from professors, not the committee.

text: Listen to an announcement at an academic conference.
script: W: Good morning, and thank you for your patience. We have had a last-minute change in the program that I'd like to explain.

W: Dr. Fernandez, who was due to give the opening talk on urban planning this morning, is stuck at the airport because her flight was delayed. She expects to arrive by lunchtime. Rather than cancel, we have swapped her talk with the one scheduled for two o'clock.

W: That means the panel on water systems now begins at half past ten in this room. If you planned to attend Dr. Fernandez's talk this morning, you might consider the workshop in Room B, which is on a similar subject.
W: Printed programs are not updated, but the corrected schedule is on the screen outside.

stem: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To cancel a talk on urban planning.
To introduce a new speaker.
To explain a modified schedule.
To praise the water panel.
explanation: The speaker announces 'a last-minute change in the program' and the swap of two talks. The urban planning talk is moved, not cancelled, and no new speaker is introduced.

stem: What can attendees interested in urban planning do this morning?
options: Go to a related workshop.
Wait for Dr. Fernandez at the airport.
Listen to the water panel at two.
Read the printed program in Room B.
explanation: The speaker suggests 'the workshop in Room B, which is on a similar subject'. The water panel now begins at half past ten, and the printed program is out of date.

text: Listen to an announcement about construction near the library.
script: W: Many of you have noticed the fence going up around the plaza. Let me explain what is happening and, more importantly, what it means for your exam preparation.

W: The plaza is being rebuilt, and the drilling will occur on weekdays from eight until four. The library says that the ground floor will be the most affected, while the fourth floor, which is the quietest, should hardly notice it.

W: The library will extend its opening hours to midnight through the exam period. The study rooms in the Humanities Building have also been opened to all students, though they have to be booked online.
W: The work is expected to continue until the end of the term, so please plan accordingly.

stem: What is the speaker's main point?
options: Students should plan their study around the noise.
The plaza will be closed for several terms.
The library will close during the exams.
Drilling will be reduced during the exam period.
explanation: She says it matters 'more importantly' what the work means for exam preparation, and then offers quiet floors, longer hours and other rooms. The library will stay open late, and the work continues until the end of term.

stem: What does the speaker suggest about the ground floor of the library?
options: It has been closed to all students.
It will be reserved for exam preparation.
It will be the loudest area.
It is quieter than the fourth floor.
explanation: She says the ground floor 'will be the most affected' by the drilling, while the fourth floor is 'the quietest'. The fourth floor is therefore the better choice, not the ground floor.

text: Listen to an announcement about tickets for a basketball game.
script: M: This is the athletics office with information about tickets for Friday's championship game. Demand has been far greater than we expected.

M: Because the arena holds only three thousand people, student tickets will be distributed by lottery. To enter, log in to the athletics page before noon tomorrow. Results will be emailed at three, and winners will have until five to confirm, or the ticket passes to someone else.
M: Each winner may claim one extra ticket for a guest, but the guest must be a current student. This rule is meant to prevent resale.
M: Students who do not win may still watch on the big screen in the Student Center, where seating is first come, first served.

stem: Why is the office using a lottery?
options: Tickets are required to enter the Student Center.
More students want tickets than there are seats.
Previous games sold too few tickets.
The arena was damaged recently.
explanation: The arena 'holds only three thousand people' and demand 'has been far greater than we expected', so seats are limited. The Student Center viewing is the alternative for those who lose.

stem: What is the purpose of requiring a guest to be a current student?
options: To reduce the cost of the arena.
To make sure each student attends alone.
To fill seats with first-year students.
To stop ticket resale.
explanation: The speaker says 'This rule is meant to prevent resale'. The rule allows one guest per winner, so students do not attend alone.

text: Listen to a recorded message from a language center.
script: W: Thank you for calling the Westbridge Language Center. Our office is currently closed, but here is information that may answer your question.

W: If you are calling about the placement test, please note that it is no longer given in person. You can take it online at any time, and it takes about forty minutes. You must finish it at least three days before your intended start date, so that we can place you in the right class.
W: Many callers ask about refunds. Tuition is refundable only until the end of the first week, and registration fees are not refundable at all.
W: Our office reopens at nine tomorrow morning. For urgent questions, you may leave a message after the tone.

stem: What does the message imply about students who want to start next Monday?
options: They may pay tuition after the first week.
They should already have taken the test.
They can take the test in person tomorrow.
They must leave a message before nine.
explanation: The test must be completed 'at least three days before your intended start date', so someone starting Monday needs to have taken it already. The test is no longer given in person.

stem: Which statement about refunds is supported by the message?
options: Some payments cannot be returned.
Fees are returned after one month.
Online tests are refunded in full.
Tuition is never refundable.
explanation: The speaker says registration fees 'are not refundable at all', while tuition is refundable for the first week. Tuition is therefore refundable in part, and the test is not mentioned in the refund policy.

text: Listen to a talk by a guide at an observatory.
script: M: Welcome, everyone. Before we step into the dome, I'd like to set expectations, since I've seen visitors leave disappointed in the past.

M: Tonight, the sky is partly clear, and the telescope will point at Saturn. Through the eyepiece, you will see a small, sharp image of the planet and its rings. It will not look like the colorful photographs you've seen online, which are made by combining many exposures.
M: There is a line, and it moves slowly, because everybody gets about a minute at the eyepiece. If clouds appear, we may have to switch to the star cluster, which is less dramatic but more reliable.
M: Please use only red flashlights in the dome, because white light ruins everyone's night vision.

stem: Why does the guide say the planet will not look like photographs?
options: To show that the telescope is old.
To explain why the line moves slowly.
To advise visitors to buy photographs.
To avoid letting visitors down.
explanation: He begins by saying he has 'seen visitors leave disappointed' and then notes the photographs are 'made by combining many exposures'. His aim is to set realistic expectations.

stem: What will probably happen if clouds cover Saturn?
options: Visitors will use white flashlights.
The visit will be cancelled for the night.
The group will look at a star cluster.
The line will move more quickly.
explanation: He says 'we may have to switch to the star cluster, which is less dramatic but more reliable'. Nothing suggests the visit would be cancelled.

text: Listen to a message from a professor about office hours.
script: W: This is Professor Mbeki. I'm sending this message to everyone in my statistics seminar, because I've noticed a pattern.

W: Over the past two weeks, almost all the students who came to my office hours did so on the day before an assignment was due. That is exactly when I can help least, since I'm usually busy answering the same question for ten people at once.
W: From now on, I'll hold extra hours on Mondays, at least three days before each deadline. If you bring a draft or a specific problem, we can accomplish a great deal in twenty minutes.
W: I'm not saying you shouldn't ask for help at the last minute. I'm saying it will be less useful.

stem: What is the professor's main purpose?
options: To refuse questions the day before deadlines.
To announce a change in assignments.
To cancel her usual office hours.
To encourage students to seek help earlier.
explanation: She notices students come 'the day before an assignment was due', which is when she can help least, and adds Monday hours 'at least three days before each deadline'. She does not refuse last-minute help.

stem: What does the professor mean by 'it will be less useful'?
options: The Monday sessions will not be helpful.
Last-minute help is less effective.
The assignments are too hard to finish.
Her answers will be wrong when she is busy.
explanation: She is contrasting last-minute help with earlier help: when she answers 'the same question for ten people at once', she can do less for each. She does not say her answers will be wrong.

text: Listen to a voicemail message from an academic advisor.
script: M: Hi Aisha, it's Mr. Brandt from the advising office, following up on our conversation yesterday.

M: I checked the course catalog, and I need to correct something I said. I told you that Organic Chemistry could be taken in your third semester, but it requires a prerequisite that you haven't completed. That could affect your plan to graduate on time.

M: The good news is that the prerequisite is offered in the summer, and most students who go this route finish without delay. The registration for summer courses closes on the twenty-fifth, though, so you can't afford to wait.
M: I'm in the office until five. Come by, or call, so we can work out the details.

stem: Why is the advisor calling Aisha?
options: To tell her she cannot graduate.
To ask her to drop a course.
To fix something he said.
To register her for classes.
explanation: He says 'I need to correct something I said' about when she could take Organic Chemistry. He does not say that she cannot graduate; he offers a way to avoid delay.

stem: What is the advisor suggesting Aisha do?
options: Take the prerequisite this summer.
Take Organic Chemistry in her third semester.
Wait for the registration to reopen.
Delay her graduation by one semester.
explanation: The prerequisite is 'offered in the summer', and registration 'closes on the twenty-fifth, so you can't afford to wait'. Taking Organic Chemistry in the third semester is what he wrongly said earlier.

text: Listen to a notice about dining services during construction.
script: W: As many of you know, the Central Dining Hall will close next Monday for renovation. I'd like to describe what will replace it, since the changes aren't all that obvious.
W: Three food trucks will park outside the Student Center from eleven until two on weekdays. Meal plan swipes will be accepted there, but each swipe covers only a main dish, not a drink.
W: The two smaller cafes, which usually sell only snacks, will serve hot lunches, though their menus will be limited. They are expected to be crowded, so we suggest avoiding noon.
W: The dining hall should reopen in January. Updated menus are on the dining services website.

stem: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To advise students to cancel meal plans.
To announce the opening of a new dining hall.
To say how students can eat.
To invite students to a food truck festival.
explanation: She describes food trucks and cafes that 'will replace' the closed dining hall. The dining hall will reopen in January, and food trucks are a temporary replacement, not a festival.

stem: What does the speaker imply about the cafes at noon?
options: They are likely to be busy.
They will serve only snacks then.
They will not accept meal plans.
They will close for cleaning.
explanation: She says the cafes 'are expected to be crowded, so we suggest avoiding noon'. Hot lunches are a change from their usual snacks, and acceptance of meal plans is not discussed.

text: Listen to an announcement about a scholarship essay.
script: W: Good afternoon. A few of you have asked about the essay for the Founders' Scholarship, so I'd like to make a short comment.

W: The prompt asks you to describe a challenge you have faced. Past winners were not necessarily those who had faced the biggest challenges. The committee tells us that the essays which impressed them most were honest about what the writer learned, and what they would do differently.
W: A common weakness is to spend the whole essay describing the difficulty and then end with a single sentence of lesson. Try to give the reflection at least as much space as the story.
W: Essays are limited to six hundred words, and are due by Friday the ninth.

stem: According to the speaker, what impressed the committee in past essays?
options: A long list of earlier achievements.
An account of an extreme difficulty.
A very detailed description of events.
Honest thoughts on what was learned.
explanation: The most impressive essays 'were honest about what the writer learned, and what they would do differently'. Past winners were 'not necessarily' those with the biggest challenges.

stem: What advice does the speaker give about the structure of the essay?
options: Keep the story to a single paragraph.
Spend as long on lessons as on events.
Begin with the lesson learned.
End with a short summary of the challenge.
explanation: She warns against ending 'with a single sentence of lesson' and advises giving 'the reflection at least as much space as the story'. She does not ask for a short story or for the lesson to come first.

text: Listen to a message inviting students to join a study about commuting.
script: M: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel from the Transportation Research Group. We are looking for students who travel to campus by bike or on foot.

M: Our interest is in how weather affects commuting choices. If you take part, we'll ask you to keep a short travel diary for two weeks, noting how you came to campus each day and why. We'll also invite you to a thirty-minute interview afterward.
M: We aren't looking for people who always cycle in all weather, nor for those who never do. We want the ones whose habits change depending on conditions.
M: If that sounds like you, send a short email to the address on our website. Participation earns a gift card.

stem: Who is the research group trying to recruit?
options: Students who cycle every day of the year.
Students who live on campus.
Those whose habits depend on weather.
Students who prefer to take the bus.
explanation: The speaker says 'We want the ones whose habits change depending on conditions'. Both people who always cycle and those who never do are excluded, and the study is about walkers and cyclists, not bus riders.

stem: What will participants do after the diary period?
options: Take part in a brief interview.
Write a report about their journeys.
Collect a gift card in person.
Complete a new two-week diary.
explanation: After the two-week diary they are invited to 'a thirty-minute interview afterward'. The gift card is a reward, and no report or second diary is mentioned.

text: Listen to a safety announcement about bicycles on campus.
script: M: Attention, cyclists. The campus police have asked me to share a few words about bike safety, especially since the new bike lane opened on Oak Avenue.

M: Many of you have welcomed the lane, and it has certainly made the ride easier. However, there have been several near misses where cyclists crossed the lane at the bus stop without looking, and where pedestrians stepped into the lane without realizing it was there.
M: The solution is simple: slow down near bus stops and crossings, and ring your bell before passing anyone.
M: Also, remember that locks are free at the campus police office, and any bike left unlocked overnight will be tagged and may be removed.

stem: What problem does the speaker describe?
options: Cyclists refusing to use the new lane.
Near collisions at crossings.
Buses blocking the lane for many hours.
Bikes being stolen from the bus stop.
explanation: He mentions 'several near misses' by cyclists crossing at the bus stop and by pedestrians stepping into the lane. The lane is welcomed, not avoided, and theft is not mentioned.

stem: What can be inferred about the new bike lane?
options: It will be closed after the safety review.
It was built to reduce pedestrian traffic.
It is only open at certain times.
